paper_title: DRBench Pro: A Knowledge-Centric Benchmark for Professional Deep Research Agents

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Deep research agents gather information from multiple sources and synthesize it into reports on complex, open-ended questions. Existing benchmarks assess report quality along several dimensions, but lack a dedicated knowledge-centric evaluation of which research directions a report covers and how deeply it explores them. We introduce DRBench Pro, a benchmark that makes structured knowledge coverage the primary evaluation target. Our automated pipeline builds local knowledge trees from Wikipedia and uses sampled subgraphs to generate research queries and evidence-grounded rubrics. Each rubric corresponds to a relation in the tree, preserving the structure of the knowledge being evaluated. Agents receive only the research query. This structure allows us to measure breadth across major research directions and depth along related knowledge chains, with their geometric mean giving overall coverage. The benchmark includes 144 cases across 24 domains and 44,102 rubrics. Evaluating 16 deep research agents reveals different strengths in breadth and depth, with the best-performing agent reaching 57.04% overall coverage. Rubric judgments agree closely with human annotations, and agent rankings remain stable across the tested metric configurations.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Deep research agents address complex, open-ended information needs through iterative search, evidence selection, and long-form synthesis. They can investigate topic across multiple sources and produce research reports that connect relevant facts, explain relationships, and organize findings into coherent account. Unlike short-form question answering, this task requires an agent to decide which research directions deserve Figure 1 Structured knowledge coverage in DRBench Pro. Evaluating deep research is challenging because open-ended questions admit multiple valid reports, while single reference answer rarely captures all relevant knowledge. Factuality checks can identify unsupported statements but cannot penalize omitted knowledge (Min et al., 2023; Wei et al., 2024; Song et al., 2024b). Existing benchmarks therefore use expert reports, reference facts, and task-specific rubrics to define expected content and assess factuality, comprehensiveness, citation quality, and writing (Du et al., 2026; Sharma et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026b). Recent approaches further reduce manual effort by generating evaluation criteria from Wikipedia, research graphs, or structured task representations (Wang et al., 2026c;d; Dong et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026a), providing explicit criteria for assessing report coverage. However, existing benchmarks lack dedicated knowledge-centric evaluation of how broadly and deeply reports cover structured reference space. Knowledge coverage is typically one component of broader assessments that also consider formatting, organization, and writing style (Du et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026b). Expert references and manually authored rubrics further limit expansion across domains, while individually specifying or checking detailed criteria makes rubric coverage costly to scale within each task. More fundamentally, even automatically generated criteria lose their relationships under flat aggregation, obscuring whether reports cover more research directions or develop selected directions more deeply. Recent treeand DAG-based approaches preserve structure for supervision, task completion, or evidence traceability (Zhu et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026a; Sun et al., 2026; Gao et al., 2026). They do not, however, explicitly treat structured knowledge coverage as their primary evaluation target. Specifically, coverage scores use topology-derived weights that are fixed in advance for each task and do not adapt to interactions among knowledge items covered in report. Yet the value of knowledge item also depends on whether it connects to related knowledge that is already covered in the report. Complete-path checks establish whether conclusions have supporting evidence, but do not provide graded measure of how far coverage extends along knowledge chain when coverage is partial or interrupted by missing intermediate relations. These limitations leave both the breadth of coverage across research directions and the depth of coverage along related knowledge chains insufficiently characterized  (Table 1)  . To fill this gap, we introduce DRBench Pro, knowledge-centric benchmark that treats structured knowledge coverage as its primary evaluation target. Our automated pipeline builds local entityrelation tree through multi-hop expansion from Wikipedia root entity and samples coherent subgraphs defining distinct research scopes. Each subgraph is used to generate both root-centered research query and rubric set. Every retained edge defines rubric grounded in Wikipedia evidence, preserving its structural position in the reference tree. This shared construction aligns task scope with evaluation units and makes each judgment traceable to its originating relation and structural position. We further propose topology-aware metrics that aggregate edge-level judgments bottom-up over the reference tree. Breadth measures how comprehensively report covers major research directions, allowing descendant coverage to partially compensate for an omitted relation. Depth measures how far reports develop related knowledge chains, with descendant credit conditioned on whether connecting relations are covered. It rewards continuity while retaining discounted credit beyond missing intermediate relations, providing graded scores for incomplete chains. Subtrees are ranked by their realized coverage in each report to emphasize well-developed chains. Their geometric mean yields overall coverage. Evaluating 16 deep research agents reveals substantially interleaved breadth and depth rankings, exposing coverage differences that single aggregate score can conceal 2 (Figure 1). The strongest evaluated agent, Claude Opus 5, achieves 57.04% overall coverage, followed by Grok 4.5 at 50.98%, leaving substantial room for improvement even among frontier agents. Rubric judgments agree with human labels at Macro-F1 of 0.893, and agent rankings remain stable under perturbations of all metric parameters. Our main contributions are as follows: We introduce DRBench Pro, knowledge-centric benchmark dedicated to structured knowledge coverage in deep research reports, comprising 144 cases across 24 domains and 44,102 evidence-grounded rubrics, built by an automated pipeline that jointly generates each research query and its hidden rubrics from the same Wikipedia-derived subgraph while preserving the evidence provenance and structural position of every rubric. We propose topology-aware breadth and depth metrics, together with overall coverage, to distinguish coverage across research directions from progression along related knowledge chains, supported by humanconsistency and stability analyses. We evaluate 16 deep research agents and identify distinct coverage strengths and remaining gaps. We also provide local research framework with fixed Wikipedia snapshot, standardized tools, and shared workflow and interaction budgets for controlled evaluation of backbone LLMs.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: Deep research evaluation. Deep research benchmarks evaluate reports through task-specific criteria covering comprehensiveness, factuality, and citation quality (Du et al., 2026; Sharma et al., 2026; Han et al., 2025; Zhong et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026b; Avraham et al., 2026). Expected content is drawn from expert reports, Wikipedia, generated criteria, or research graphs, with varying degrees of automation in task and rubric construction (Li et al., 2026b; Wang et al., 2026c;d; Dong et al., 2026). For survey-based reports, referenceliterature recall and statement veracity measure source coverage and factual accuracy (Li et al., 2025b). Complementary evaluations examine information gathering through broad exploration, passage-retrieval completeness, and exhaustive collection (Java et al., 2026; Kim et al., 2026; Wong et al., 2026; Gupta et al., 2026). Factuality and content coverage. Factuality and coverage address complementary questions: whether reported claims are supported, and whether relevant information is missing. Claim-level verification and citation audits check generated statements against evidence (Min et al., 2023; Wei et al., 2024; Song et al., 2024b; Gao et al., 2023; Venkit et al., 2025), while joint analysis of retrieval and generation helps locate failures in systems that use retrieved evidence (Ru et al., 2024). Coverage evaluation instead identifies omissions by comparing outputs with reference content units and key facts (Nenkova & Passonneau, 2004; Liu et al., 2023; Song et al., 2024a; Lee et al., 2024), testing whether they answer reference questions (Deutsch et al., 2021; Scialom et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2024; Tan et al., 2024), or checking for salient aspects and insights across documents (Samarinas et al., 2025; Pradeep et al., 2025; Laban et al., 2024). Automated rubric generation and judgment calibration support the construction and application of these evaluation criteria (Rao & Callison-Burch, 2026; Hashemi et al., 2024). Structured construction and evaluation. Graphs and trees organize multi-hop questions (Welbl et al., 2018; Yang et al., 2018; Ho et al., 2020; Trivedi et al., 2022; Zhu et al., 2024) and synthetic web-search tasks (Li et al., 2025a; Lu et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025; Tao et al., 2025; 2026; Li et al., 2026a). For deep research, they connect queries, evidence, and rubrics to support reinforcement learning supervision and propagation of rubric weights (Zhu et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026a). Structured evidence also enables tracing across research stages and depth and width tests for system comparison (Sun et al., 2026; Gao et al., 2026). Using structure to construct tasks or trace evidence is distinct from retaining it to aggregate report coverage. Our benchmark makes structured knowledge coverage the primary evaluation target: each rubric retains its position in an 3 Figure 2 Overview of DRBench Pro. (A) We construct Wikipedia-derived local graph around selected root entity and sample subgraphs by retaining selected children of the root and their complete descendant subtrees together with the root. (B1) Each sampled subgraph defines research query. (B2) Each sampled edge is converted into an edge-grounded rubric, forming the hidden rubric set. (C) An evaluated deep research agent answers the query with report; judge scores the report against the rubric set, and the edge-level scores are mapped back to the local knowledge tree and aggregated bottom-up into breadth and depth. entityrelation tree during aggregation, yielding separate breadth and depth measures for coverage across research directions and along related knowledge chains. sections.title: 3 Benchmark Construction and Evaluation Protocol
sections.content: Measuring knowledge coverage requires reference that specifies both what report could cover and how that knowledge is organized. We introduce DRBench Pro, which uses Wikipedia-derived knowledge trees to define research tasks and their evaluation criteria within shared reference space. The tree structure separates major research directions from chains of related knowledge within them, enabling distinct measures of breadth and depth. Figure 2 illustrates the construction and evaluation pipeline. The prompts used for benchmark construction and evaluation are provided in Appendix J.

sections.title: 3.1 Wikipedia-derived Local Graph Construction
sections.content: A reference space for knowledge coverage needs to connect research topics with supporting evidence. Wikipedia provides linked entities whose relationships can be examined in their source context. To span diverse domains, we adopt all 24 topic categories from WebOrganizer (Wettig et al., 2025) and select two root entities per category. Each root has sufficiently detailed, reliably parseable article and enough outgoing links to support expansion. Starting from each root, we expand Wikipedia links breadth-first. Nodes represent entities, and edges represent relationships supported by link anchors and surrounding text. We organize the retained expansion as rooted tree, with one parent per non-root node and unique path from the root. This structure gives each relation an identifiable position for subsequent rubric construction and coverage aggregation. Distance from the root is measured by the number of links along this path, and expansion stops at three hops. To provide diverse candidate research directions while bounding the size of deeper expansions, we retain 50 children of the root and at most five children of each other node. Invalid or duplicate candidates are filtered 4 before Claude Opus 4.8 selects neighbors for their relevance to the current entity and usefulness for research tasks. The resulting 48 local knowledge trees contain approximately 1.5K nodes each on average. Appendix reports detailed statistics, and Appendix C.1 analyzes the choice of two roots per domain. Model-call costs for construction are reported in Appendix H.

sections.title: 3.2 Subgraph Sampling
sections.content: A full knowledge tree spans more material than single research request can reasonably target. We therefore sample smaller subgraphs, each defining the scope of one research case. branch consists of one child of the root and all its descendants: it represents research direction, while paths within it capture chains of related knowledge. Each case retains the root and 10 complete branches, preserving the knowledge structure within the selected directions. To make each scope coherent, Claude Opus 4.8 jointly selects three groups of branches from each tree, using the candidate entities page summaries, relations to the root, and descendant information. Branches within group are selected to provide complementary perspectives on common research task; the three groups do not share root branches. Retaining complete branches preserves the deeper relations needed to evaluate coverage within each direction. This yields three cases per root and 144 cases across the 24 domains.

sections.title: 3.3 Query and Rubric Construction
sections.content: The research request and its evaluation criteria should refer to the same knowledge scope. We therefore use Claude Opus 4.8 to generate both the query and the rubrics from each sampled subgraph. For query generation, the model receives the root entity and the sampled knowledge scope, and is instructed to frame natural research request around their broader themes. The prompt discourages listing hidden entities or restating the subgraph as checklist, so the agent is asked to investigate topic rather than reproduce an explicit answer outline. To make the expected coverage traceable to evidence, we create one rubric per retained relation edge. Each rubric asks whether the report covers the relationship between its source and target entities. The generator uses only the supplied evidence: page summaries, the anchor sentence, relevant paragraphs, and available backlink context from the two pages. This ties each scoring requirement to documented content rather than an unsupported model-generated expectation. Each rubric retains its edges position in the reference tree, allowing its judgment to be aggregated with those of related rubrics. We also record its hop distance as the distance from the root to the edges target node for structural diagnostics. These annotations are kept outside the rubric text. Evaluated agents receive only the query; the reference tree and rubrics remain hidden.

sections.title: 3.4 Topology-aware Knowledge Coverage Evaluation
sections.content: Counting satisfied rubrics alone can give similar scores to reports with different coverage patterns. We therefore retain the reference tree when aggregating judgments, distinguishing coverage across research directions from coverage along related knowledge chains. An LLM judge assigns each hidden rubric one of three verdicts: Satisfied, Partially Satisfied, or Not Satisfied. For coverage metric computation, we map Satisfied to 1 (covered) and both Partially Satisfied and Not Satisfied to 0 (uncovered). These binary values are then aggregated over the reference tree. Breadth. Breadth measures how comprehensively report covers the selected research directions. We give these directions equal weight so that branch with more rubrics does not dominate the score. Within branch, deeper relations can demonstrate coverage of direction even when shallower relation is missing. We preserve each relations direct score as weighted component and use the mean breadth of its child subtrees to account for descendant coverage. Averaging the resulting branch scores gives case-level breadth. 5 Depth. Depth measures coverage along related knowledge chains in the reference tree. report can cover one chain deeply without covering every branch equally, so we give greater weight to child subtrees with higher depth scores while retaining smaller contributions from the others. Each relation contributes its own score and regulates how much descendant coverage is credited: an uncovered intermediate relation reduces that credit without discarding it. This rewards continuity along knowledge chains. We apply the same rank-based weighting across the selected research directions to obtain case-level depth. Appendix C.5 analyzes the textual organization of supporting evidence for consecutive satisfied rubrics. Overall coverage. We combine case-level breadth Bc and depth Dc through their geometric mean, Sc = BcDc, (1) so weak coverage in either dimension lowers the combined score. Each of the three metrics is then averaged separately across the 144 cases. Both metrics are computed from the leaves toward the root, starting with the direct rubric scores and recursively combining them with descendant coverage. Appendix provides the complete procedure in Algorithm 1, together with the equations, parameter definitions, and boundary conventions.

sections.title: 4.1 Evaluation Setup
sections.content: Evaluation methods. We evaluate 16 deep research agents and group them into three categories according to how search and research orchestration are provided. (1) Deep Research Systems. These are end-to-end research agents explicitly designed for autonomous, long-horizon investigation. They natively combine planning, iterative evidence gathering, and long-form synthesis. We evaluate o3 Deep Research, Perplexity Sonar Deep Research, and Qwen Deep Research. (2) Native Search LLMs. These models integrate provider-native web search directly into generation without relying on separate Deep Research product workflow. We evaluate Grok 4.5, Claude Opus 5, GPT-5.6 Sol, Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview, Sonar Reasoning Pro, and Qwen3.8 Max with native web search enabled. (3) Backbone LLMs under the local research framework. As controlled and reproducible evaluation setting, we implement the local research framework backed by the fixed English Wikipedia dump enwiki-20260701-v1. The framework exposes Search and Open operations over the same snapshot, disables provider-native web search, and keeps the research workflow and budget fixed across backbone LLMs. Its purpose is to provide common search service into which different backbone LLMs can be integrated, rather than to improve their benchmark scores. This design removes temporal drift in the retrieval corpus, reduces variation from external search infrastructure, and retains auditable evidence records. We evaluate Gemma 4 31B, DeepSeek V4 Pro, DeepSeek V4 Flash, Qwen3.8 Max, Qwen3.7 Plus, GLM 5.2, and MiniMax M3 as backbone LLMs. The execution protocol and formal configuration of the local research framework are detailed in Appendix F. Appendix D.5 evaluates LangChain Open Deep Research with DeepSeek V4 Flash on small sample. Implementation details. The evaluated reports were collected during the periods listed in Appendix G. We use Gemini 2.5 Pro as the judge for the formal evaluation. It assigns each rubric one of three verdicts: Satisfied, Partially Satisfied, or Not Satisfied. We retain these original judgments and convert them into binary rubric scores of 0 or 1 for the metrics in Section 3.4. sections.title: 4.2 Evaluation Results
sections.content: Overall performance. Table 2 shows that Claude Opus 5 achieves the highest overall coverage (57.04%) and ranks first in both breadth (53.09%) and depth (61.91%), yielding strong performance in both dimensions. Grok 4.5 and o3 Deep Research follow, with relatively stronger breadth and depth, respectively. High overall coverage therefore requires both comprehensive coverage across major directions and progress along related knowledge chains. Appendix C.3 lists selected results from prior benchmarks for context. Interleaved breadthdepth profiles. The agent orderings differ substantially between breadth and depth, revealing distinct research strengths and showing that research workflows can produce markedly different coverage profiles. The clearest example is Qwen3.8 Max: under the local research framework, its breadth and depth scores are 15.54 and 6.28 percentage points higher, respectively, than under its Native Search configuration, with the difference concentrated primarily in breadth. The two configurations of the same-named model therefore exhibit different knowledge-exploration patterns: the local research framework configuration covers major research directions more comprehensively, whereas the depth difference is comparatively limited. similar contrast appears within the Perplexity product line: Perplexity Sonar Deep Research attains higher depth but slightly lower breadth than Sonar Reasoning Pro. Together, these results show that breadth and depth expose agent specializations and research-strategy differences that overall coverage alone cannot reveal. 7 Figure 4 Overall coverage across domains. Values are percentages. Orange indicates higher scores, while blue indicates lower scores. Figure 3 presents two representative cases. For Lew Grade, similar overall coverage masks breadthdepth trade-off. For Temperance, agents can deepen their investigations along different knowledge paths. Appendix presents the case studies in greater detail. Appendix E.4 provides full report with rubric judgments and highlighted evidence. Coverage under the local research framework. Under the local research framework, Qwen3.8 Max achieves the highest overall coverage (47.94%). Several backbone LLMs remain competitive under limited budget. Among the leading backbones, breadth scores are already relatively close, whereas differences in depth further separate their overall coverage. Because these models share the same knowledge source, workflow, tool-use constraints, and budget, the remaining differences reflect backbone-dependent behavior in task decomposition, tool use, evidence selection, and report synthesis. Appendix D.2 analyzes the agents research trajectories. Appendices D.3 and D.4 analyze length sensitivity and retrieval-to-report knowledge retention.

sections.title: 4.3 Coverage Profiles across Domains
sections.content: Figure 4 shows overall coverage across 24 domains, with each agentdomain score averaged over six cases. Across agents, coverage is highest in Software Development (53.69%), Science & Technology (52.36%), and Health (50.10%), and lowest in Industrial (28.58%) and Food & Dining (35.45%). Claude Opus 5 leads in 23 domains, and o3 Deep Research leads in Literature. Appendix D.1 provides the corresponding breadth and depth profiles.

sections.title: 4.4 Research Task Quality and Leakage
sections.content: Because each research query is generated from sampled subgraph, we manually review all 144 queries using three criteria: research value, public answerability, and alignment with their assigned domains  (Table 3)  . The three Medium cases arise from natural cross-domain overlap, as subgraph sampling produces topic-specific research scopes that are not necessarily confined to single domain; the queries nevertheless remain coherent, publicly answerable, and sufficiently aligned with their assigned domains for benchmark evaluation. sections.title: 5 Conclusion
sections.content: We introduce DRBench Pro, knowledge-centric benchmark for professional deep research agents. From each sampled multi-hop Wikipedia-derived entity subgraph, it jointly generates research query and traceable edgegrounded rubrics, giving the case, knowledge scope, and evaluation criteria shared structural foundation. Topology-aware aggregation captures breadth across major research directions and depth along related knowledge chains, with their geometric mean yielding overall coverage. Evaluation across 16 deep research agents reveals interleaved breadthdepth profiles; with the knowledge source, workflow, tool interface, and interaction budget fixed, the local research framework further distinguishes the coverage behavior of different backbone LLMs. Overall, DRBench Pro uses graph topology in both benchmark construction and metric formulation, providing scalable, structure-aware foundation for evaluating knowledge coverage in deep research reports.

Larger samples provide only modest further improvements. We therefore select two roots per domain and use the resulting 144-case benchmark. 18 C.2 Research Query Quality Criteria Research Value. This criterion asks whether the query warrants research report. strong query calls for substantive investigation, retrieval, and synthesis across relevant evidence; request answerable through short factual lookup has limited research value. Public Answerability. This criterion asks whether reliable, publicly available sources can, in principle, support an answer to the query. The answer need not appear in single source, but the requested findings must be verifiable without private information or unsupported speculation. QueryDomain Match. This criterion asks whether the querys central topic and requested analysis fit its assigned domain. The domain is shown alongside the query during review. Cross-domain connections are compatible with match when the assigned domain remains central; merely incidental connection is insufficient. C.3 Additional Results from Prior Benchmarks Table 13 compiles selected results from prior benchmarks, focusing on model families represented in Table 2 and evaluation dimensions with definitions similar to ours. These results serve as an external reference for our evaluation, with each row labeled by its operating setting in the source study. Setting 1 (Deep Research product) denotes an end-to-end research product or system that integrates research planning, iterative retrieval, and report generation. Setting 2 (native search / search tools) denotes model using native search or search tools during generation. Setting 3 (external framework + backbone) denotes backbone model embedded in an external retrieval or research framework that organizes tool calls and the research workflow. These labels describe the source experiments; the same model can use different settings across studies. In HiEviDR (Sun et al., 2026), 3R and 3D denote the RAG and Deep Research workflows, respectively. For ResearchRubrics (Sharma et al., 2026), we report binary compliance on tasks with high conceptual breadth or deep logical nesting; DR-Arenas Depth/Width values describe the composition of failure types, rather than standalone ability scores (Gao et al., 2026). Cross-benchmark comparisons require accounting for differences in experimental settings, model versions, and metric definitions. Studies may use different retrieval resources, tool interfaces, and execution budgets; evaluations conducted at different times often cover different versions within the same model family; and even similarly named metrics may differ in their reference content, scoring criteria, and aggregation rules. We therefore compare relative performance trends among related models and interpret agreement and variation in light of these conditions. For model pairs with relatively clear correspondences, our results agree with several prior studies. In Table 2, o3 Deep Research achieves higher overall coverage than Perplexity Sonar Deep Research. The corresponding OpenAIPerplexity product-family ordering also appears in the selected dimensions of DeepResearch Bench (Du et al., 2026), DeepResearch Bench II (Li et al., 2026b), ResearchRubrics, Wiki Live Challenges Broad metric (Wang et al., 2026c), DeepResearchEval (Wang et al., 2026d), and LiveResearchBench (Wang et al., 2026b). The advantage of o3 Deep Research over Qwen Deep Research is also consistent with the corresponding product-family results in DeepResearch Bench II, Wiki Live Challenge, and DeepResearchEval. Among native-search models, LiveResearchBench orders GPT-5 above Gemini 2.5 Pro and Sonar Reasoning Pro, matching the overall-coverage order of the corresponding model families in Table 2. Although versions and protocols differ, these recurring relative advantages provide useful external context for our results. Despite these recurring trends, some metrics and model pairs exhibit different relative orderings, including Wiki Live Challenges Cov. Wiki, Super Researchs Coverage (Dong et al., 2026), and the GLM-5.2DeepSeek-V4Pro comparison in From Simple QA to Deep Research (Wang et al., 2026a). Taken together, these comparisons show that our evaluation recovers several relative performance trends reported in prior benchmarks, providing complementary evidence for its validity. 19 Table 13 Selected results from prior benchmarks. sections.title: E Case Study
sections.content: We use three diagnostic cases to connect aggregate scores to concrete report behavior. The first requires similar overall coverage with crossed breadthdepth profile; the second examines reports that follow largely different chains of related knowledge within the same research space; and the third is restricted to the unified local research framework and contrasts higher research activity with lower coverage performance. E.1 Similar Overall Coverage Can Hide Different Research Strategies Query. Im trying to understand the career of the British entertainment mogul Lew Grade, particularly his transition from television into big-budget international film production during the 1970s and early 1980s. Id like well-researched overview that explains how his instincts and financing strategies produced both remarkable successes and costly failures, and how these outcomes shaped his reputation and financial standing over time. Rather than just listing his projects, Im interested in the bigger picture: why he pursued ambitious, prestige, and family-oriented entertainment for global audiences, how his partnerships with major directors and creative figures worked in practice, and what balance of artistic risk and commercial calculation drove his decisions. Id also like to understand how combination of overreach and shifting business pressures eventually undermined his control of his own company and led to corporate takeover. Please connect his personal management style to the broader changes in how film and television were financed and distributed during his era, and assess how his legacy has been judged. Perplexity Sonar Deep Research and Grok 4.5 obtain similar overall coverage on this case (38.83 vs. 40.31), despite exhibiting sharply inverted coverage profiles. Perplexity Sonar Deep Research covers major research directions less comprehensively but follows chains of related knowledge farther within selected directions (breadth 27.33, depth 55.19). By contrast, Grok 4.5 exhibits the opposite pattern (breadth 54.48, depth 29.82). Figure 8 shows how these contrasting profiles can yield similar overall coverage scores. This case illustrates general limitation of scalar report evaluation: similar aggregate performance does not imply similar research behavior. One report covers major research directions more comprehensively, while the other follows chains of related knowledge farther within selected directions. 28 Figure 8 Similar overall coverage can conceal different research strategies. Bars show aggregate breadth and depth (%). Gray rays mark ten shared research directions. Colored ray width and opacity encode branch breadth, while ray length encodes branch depth. Figure 9 Deep research can explore different knowledge paths. Values above the models report overall coverage, breadth, and depth (%). Matched gray rays mark the same research directions. Colored ray width and opacity encode branch breadth, while ray length encodes branch depth. E.2 Deep Research Can Explore Different Knowledge Paths Query. Im trying to understand the temperance movement not just as campaign against alcohol, but as broad historical phenomenon that grew out of specific social conditions and then spread and changed in surprising ways. Id like research-style report that traces how early alarm over heavy drinking in one society, combined with new medical and moral arguments, laid the groundwork for organized reform. Im especially curious about how different religious traditions shaped competing versions of the movement, giving it distinct doctrinal flavors and leaders, and how this influenced its appeal across communities. Beyond its origins in Britain and America, Id like to understand how the movement traveled to colonial and settler societies, where it became entangled with other causes like womens political rights and, strikingly, with anti-colonial and independence struggles and religious revivals. Please explain how these motivations interacted, why the same idea took on such different meanings in different places, and what tensions or contradictions emerged as it evolved, without simply listing every organization or figure involved. Reports on the same question may emphasize different directions and knowledge chains even when their 29 aggregate scores are similar. On this case, o3 Deep Research and GPT-5.6 Sol achieve breadth scores of 32.11 and 34.64, depth scores of 48.26 and 50.43, and overall coverage scores of 39.37 and 41.79, respectively. Despite these similar aggregate results, their branch-level coverage profiles differ substantially. Figure 9 summarizes both reports across the same ten research directions, making their differing emphases visible. This case illustrates how reports on the same question can emphasize different parts of the underlying knowledge space. Branch-level analysis makes these differences visible by showing each reports progression along knowledge chains within individual directions. E.3 More Research Activity Does Not Guarantee Higher Coverage Query. Id like well-researched cultural history of Horn & Hardart, the automat chain, that goes beyond describing how the vending-style restaurants worked and instead examines why this company became such durable fixture in American popular imagination. Im especially curious about how the company built its public presence through sponsorship of broadcast entertainment in the early days of radio, including how those programs helped launch performers who later became famous, and how that kind of promotional and media involvement shaped its brand. Second, Id like to understand why writers, songwriters, filmmakers, and stage productions kept referencing or recreating its dining rooms across decades and what the automat came to symbolize about class, city life, and nostalgia in songs, comedies, and films. Finally, please connect its rise and eventual decline to broader shifts in urban dining, entertainment, and changing tastes, so the report reads as an interpretive account of its lasting legacy rather than just timeline of locations and menu items. Table 24 summarizes the research activity, report length, and coverage scores of GLM 5.2 and DeepSeek V4 Flash on this case. Under the same frozen corpus, tool interface, workflow, and action budgets, GLM 5.2 makes more Search and Open calls, retrieves more pages, and uses more tokens, with part of its effort devoted to revisiting shared sources and expanding contextual discussion. Its report is also longer, yet DeepSeek V4 Flash achieves higher breadth, depth, and overall coverage. This case shows that greater research activity and longer reports do not necessarily imply higher knowledge coverage, highlighting the importance of effective planning and evidence selection. The example thus makes both deeper coverage and continuity along the reference chains directly inspectable. Logical coherence across sections. Consecutive parentchild rubrics in the reference tree can be satisfied by evidence from different report sections while still corresponding to logically connected knowledge. For R1R5, R1 is satisfied in the section that describes how Rogue was developed and widely distributed, explaining how it became the genres defining model. R5 is satisfied in the subsequent section that discusses early roguelike variants and their developers, describing how Hacks creator attempted to recreate Rogue from memory. The discussion progresses from establishing Rogues foundational role to showing how its design influenced specific successor, preserving the continuous reasoning across the section boundary and thus demonstrating meaningful depth. Similarly, R10 and R11 connect Beneath Apple Manors position before Rogue with its early use of procedural generation, bringing together complementary historical and technical information from separate sections. Informative omissions in otherwise covered branches. R6 and R12 identify specific gaps despite coverage of their parent relations. R6 asks about Hacks cross-platform ports and their use of graphical tiles, directly addressing the querys interest in display constraints and platform changes. The reports discussion of graphical tiles in Beneath Apple Manor does not satisfy this Hack-specific requirement. R12 asks about predefined seeds for generating large worlds; describing randomized dungeons alone does not explain this mechanism. R12 offers an optional technical extension to the discussion of memory-constrained design. Although unmet in this report, these rubrics remain valuable for the task, helping distinguish reports by the specificity and completeness of their knowledge coverage.

sections.title: F Local Research Framework
sections.content: The local research framework provides common retrieval and orchestration setting for evaluating backbone LLMs. It standardizes the evidence corpus, tool interface, research stages, and interaction budget while leaving planning decisions, tool-use choices, and report generation to each backbone. Figure 11 summarizes the resulting workflow. Figure 11 Local research framework workflow. The backbone LLM decomposes the research query into three Research Units, which execute concurrently against the shared frozen Wikipedia snapshot through Search and Open. Their evidence notes undergo one coverage-gap check; when material gap is found, at most one Gap Unit collects supplemental evidence before the original query and all collected notes are synthesized into the final report. F.1 Retrieval Environment and Tool Interface All evaluations under the local research framework use the fixed English Wikipedia snapshot enwiki20260701-v1. The report generator receives the benchmark query. Provider-native web search is disabled, so every backbone searches the same time-invariant evidence space through the frameworks local tools. The framework exposes two operations over this snapshot. Search and Open serve distinct roles: Search identifies potentially relevant Wikipedia pages, whereas Open reads their contents. Given source identifier and cursor position, Open returns bounded text span. If additional text remains, it also returns next_cursor that can be used to retrieve the subsequent span. All backbone LLMs use the same tool schemas, although they independently decide what to search for and which sources to read. F.2 Research Workflow and Formal Configuration Table 26 summarizes the configuration of our local research framework used for the seven backbone LLMs in the main experiments. Table 26 Key local research framework configuration. The same settings are used for all seven backbone LLMs evaluated under the framework. Given benchmark query, planner first decomposes the task into exactly three non-overlapping Research Units, each defined by short title and bounded objective. The three initial Units execute concurrently. Within each Unit, the backbone uses Search and Open to investigate its assigned objective under fixed round and tool budgets, then returns concise evidence notes rather than complete report. This decomposition preserves common research structure while allowing each backbone to decide which queries to issue and which pages to read. After the initial Units finish, the framework performs one coverage-gap check over the query and collected evidence Parameter Value Wikipedia snapshot Retrieval tools Provider-native web search Initial Research Units Concurrent Research Units Gap Units Total Research Units Model rounds per Unit Tool calls per Unit Search calls per Unit Open calls per Unit Open calls per model turn Retrieved content per Open call At most 6,000 characters enwiki-20260701-v1 Search and Open Disabled 3 3 At most 1 At most 4 7 At most 15 At most 3 At most 12 At most 4 40 notes. If the check identifies material missing direction that can be investigated within the frozen Wikipedia snapshot, it creates one supplemental Gap Unit. The workflow therefore executes three Units by default and at most four Units in total, providing bounded second stage of evidence collection without changing the protocol across backbone LLMs. Finally, the synthesis stage receives the original query and the evidence notes produced by the Research Units and combines them into coherent Markdown report. The resulting report is subsequently scored with the same rubric set and judge protocol used for all evaluated agents.

sections.title: I Human Annotation Protocol
sections.content: I.1 Rubric-level annotation Annotators and annotation procedure. The annotations support the rubric-level humanjudge comparison in Section 4.5. Ten PhD-level annotators participated in the human evaluation. The annotation sample comprised 3,695 reportrubric pairs from 12 reports, with each report representing different benchmark domain. Under the annotation protocol, each pair receives two independent initial labels. Annotators do not have access to one anothers labels or the LLM judges verdicts. third annotator adjudicates disagreements using the relevant report passages and the same annotation criteria, producing the final human reference. Annotation criteria. Each reportrubric pair received one of three labels: Satisfied, Partially Satisfied, or Not Satisfied. Satisfied indicates that the report explicitly states or clearly paraphrases the rubrics required knowledge, including its essential relation and qualifications. Partially Satisfied indicates that the report covers substantive part of the requirement but omits an essential detail or qualification. Not Satisfied indicates that the required knowledge is absent; merely mentioning related entity or discussing the general topic does not constitute coverage. Judgments concern content present in the report, without filling gaps from external knowledge. Figure 12 illustrates the annotation interface during the report review process. Agreement and judge comparison. Initial inter-annotator agreement was Cohens κ = 0.841, computed before adjudication over all 3,695 reportrubric pairs using the original three-category labels. The resulting human-reviewed labels serve as the reference for comparison with three LLM judges. We compare the judges original three-category verdicts with this reference. For the binary comparison, Satisfied is mapped to 1 (covered), while Partially Satisfied and Not Satisfied are mapped to 0 (uncovered), for both human and judge labels. Macro-F1 is computed separately for each report and then averaged equally across the 12 reports. 42 Figure 12 Human annotation interface. Annotators assign Satisfied, Partially Satisfied, or Not Satisfied to each reportrubric pair. I.2 Report-level expert assessment The report-level assessment in Section 4.5 comprises 72 reports from six deep research agents across 12 cases from distinct domains. Each case includes six reports answering the same research query. Ten PhDlevel annotators participate in this assessment. For each case, the same three annotators from this pool independently rate all six reports on breadth, depth, and overall quality using 110 integer scale, and their mean ratings serve as the human reference. Annotators assess reports without access to agent identities, automatically computed scores, or one anothers ratings. Differences among annotators are reflected in the mean rating.

sections.title: J Prompt Templates
sections.content: We release the prompts used for benchmark construction and for evaluation to enable reproducibility and independent analysis. J.1 Benchmark Construction Prompts J.1.1 Root Entity Neighbor Selection This prompt selects the children of the root from candidate entities extracted across its complete Wikipedia page. System Prompt You are selecting set of directly related first-hop entities from the candidate links found in the full page of core Wikipedia topic. These entities will become the main directions for later deep-research tasks, so you should balance direct relationship to the core topic, aspect coverage, and later composability. Return ONLY JSON that follows the required schema. The JSON object MUST contain exactly two top-level keys: selected_candidate_ids and selected_neighbors. Rules: 43 1. Candidate scope and count: choose entities only from the provided candidate_neighbors. The selection scope is the full-article candidate pool, including both lead-section and body-section candidates. If there are at least target_neighbor_count available unique candidates, return target_neighbor_count unique candidates. Return fewer only when the candidate list itself contains fewer available unique candidates than the target. 2. Selection objective: choose candidates that best support future root-centered deep-research tasks. Value here means research usefulness, aspect coverage, and composability for broad knowledge-coverage evaluation. 3. Coverage, combination, and duplicate filtering: prefer candidates that cover different research aspects of the root, and avoid concentrating on one narrow direction. Exclude highly similar titles, aliases, repeated directions, and obvious-common-knowledge or low-information candidates such as incidental mentions, dates, generic list pages, or weak parenthetical references. Form differentiated branch set suitable for systematic DeepResearch. 4. Output structure: put the canonical selection in selected_candidate_ids. For each id in selected_candidate_ids, include exactly one object with the same candidate_id in selected_neighbors; each selected neighbor object MUST contain only candidate_id and relation_explanation. 5. Relationship explanation: relation_explanation MUST be one concise sentence explaining the relationship between the root and the selected entity, and it MUST be based only on that candidates anchor_text and context_text.

sections.title: User Prompt
sections.content: Select first-hop root expansion entities for the following Wikipedia root. root_title: {root_title} root_summary: {root_summary} target_neighbor_count: {target_neighbor_count} candidate_neighbors: {candidate_neighbors} Return ONLY JSON. J.1.2 Non-root Entity Neighbor Selection This prompt selects bounded outgoing neighbors for expanding non-root entity. System Prompt Given source Wikipedia page and the candidate links from its full article, select the outgoing entities that are best suited as next-layer expansion topics. These entities should be central and directly related to the source topic, and they should provide valuable evidence entry points for the later research scope. Return ONLY JSON that follows the required schema. Rules: 1. Select from the full source-article candidate pool, including both lead-section and body-section candidates. You may choose only from the provided candidate_neighbors. 2. Choose the candidates that are most semantically central, most directly related to the source entity, and most useful for expanding understanding of it. 3. If the candidate count is at least target_neighbor_count, return exactly target_neighbor_count unique candidates. 4. Return only selected_candidate_ids. User Prompt Select the best outgoing neighbors for the following source node. source_title: {source_title} source_depth: {source_depth} source_summary: {source_summary} target_neighbor_count: {target_neighbor_count} 44 candidate_neighbors: {candidate_neighbors} Return ONLY JSON. J.1.3 Subgraph Sampling This prompt groups the children of the root to select branches that form coherent and complementary subgraphs for downstream task construction.

sections.title: System Prompt
sections.content: You are selecting and combining candidate directions that are directly connected to core Wikipedia topic, forming several subtopic sets suitable for deep research. Each set should feel like natural research scope: its internal directions should be related and complementary, able to support later research-question framing, evidence organization, and evaluation of whether report covers key knowledge relationships. Return ONLY JSON that follows the required schema. Rules: 1. When the candidate pool allows it, construct exactly target_subgraphs groups; when the candidate pool allows it, each group should contain exactly depth_1_branches_per_subgraph unique candidates. Choose only from the provided depth-1 candidate list. 2. Each group should form coherent research scope: the selected first-hop branches should have semantic, historical, institutional, causal, comparative, or conceptual connections, and should be able to support natural deepresearch report. Do not simply choose the first candidates. Prefer branches whose descendant tree is more likely to provide effective supporting evidence. 3. Branches within group should be complementary. Avoid homogeneous branches, near duplicates, or branches that can be represented by the same angle. Unless the seed topic naturally connects them, do not combine unrelated incidental mentions. 4. Different groups should overlap as little as possible. If overlap is unavoidable, prefer reusing candidates that have the most direct relationship to the seed/root, can connect multiple research angles, and whose descendant tree is more likely to provide effective supporting evidence. 5. Use selected_candidate_ids as the canonical output. User Prompt Select depth-1 branch groups for subgraph construction. seed_entity: {seed_entity} root_summary: {root_summary} target_subgraphs: {target_subgraphs} depth_1_branches_per_subgraph: {depth_1_branches_per_subgraph} candidate_count: {candidate_count} depth_1_candidates: {depth_1_candidates} Return ONLY JSON. J.1.4 Research Query Generation This prompt converts the hidden sampled scope into research query centered on the root entity while preventing entity-list leakage. System Prompt You convert set of hidden entity-relation clues into research question that an outside user might ask. Your task is to write ONE research-style query centered on the seed/root entity. This query will be given to downstream DeepResearch model to generate report, and coverage will be evaluated using rubrics corresponding 45 to the hidden clues. subgraph_nodes is hidden construction context: use it only to understand the overall topical composition and depth profile. The final query must still present the root/seed entity as the explicit central topic. Return ONLY JSON that follows the required schema. The JSON object MUST contain exactly one top-level key: query. Rules: 1. Central topic: the final query MUST clearly center on seed_entity; the seed/root entity name may appear. The query should use the full hidden context to form research task, rather than only asking about the root article itself. 2. Anti-leakage: the final query MUST NOT directly mention any entity name in forbidden_entity_names, any exact title from depth_1_branch_inputs, or any exact title from subgraph_nodes except the seed/root entity. Also avoid semantic leakage: do not rewrite hidden candidate entities, node titles, summaries, or relation explanations into downstream-facing concrete topics, mechanisms, institutions, places, events, works, methods, people, effects, or checklists. Deeper hidden entities may not all appear in the forbidden list, but the query should still not read like an entity checklist. 3. Writing style: imitate thoughtful but non-expert user asking for research help. The query should be specific and purposeful, but should not make the user appear to know hidden entities, internal technical terms, hidden graph structure, or specific field methods. Use natural-language paragraph. 4. Source of specificity: the query should usually be one coherent paragraph, around 100-200 words in English or similar level of detail in the target language. It must not be too short or too generic, and it must not become specific by enumerating hidden candidate directions. Specificity should come from root-centered research framing, such as causal relationships, historical development, changes in evidence and interpretation, interactions among different forces, or how internal practices and external pressures shaped development. User Prompt Generate query from the hidden construction context below. query_gen_mode: {query_gen_mode} graph_metadata: {graph_metadata} seed_entity: {seed_entity} subgraph_overview: {subgraph_overview} root_node: {root_node} subgraph_nodes: {subgraph_nodes} depth_1_branch_inputs: {depth_1_branch_inputs} forbidden_entity_names: {forbidden_entity_names} Important: - The hidden node set is rooted at seed_entity. - The root node is depth 0. - Each subgraph_nodes item contains node id, Wikipedia title, and root-hop depth. - smaller depth means fewer knowledge hops from the root and usually closer structural relationship to it. - The final query should be research task based on the full hidden context while staying centered on the root entity. - Node titles are hidden construction evidence and must not become topic checklist in the final query. Return ONLY JSON. J.1.5 Rubric Generation This prompt converts each edge in case subgraph into an evaluation rubric based on its associated evidence. System Prompt You will receive batch of relationship records, each made from source entity and target entity. Each record includes evidence from Wikipedia page summaries and relationship context. Your task is to write one verifiable knowledge-coverage requirement for each record, so that later research report can be checked for whether it clearly covers the specific knowledge relationship expressed by that record. 46 For each relationship record, use only the materials provided by that record: source page summary, target page summary, and relation evidence sentence / paragraph. Do not use internal structural information such as node depth, path position, centrality, or subgraph topology. Return ONLY JSON that follows the required schema. Rules: 1. Generate exactly one rubric object for each provided rubric_id. 2. Each rubric must be faithful to that relationship records own source/target/evidence materials, and must be written as knowledge coverage requirement for report content, not as writing-quality judgment. 3. The rubric must be based on the provided page summaries and relationship evidence. Do not invent claims beyond the summaries and relation evidence. If the evidence is weak, keep the rubric narrow and concrete. If the evidence sentence supports clear relationship, prefer explicit relation coverage. report may satisfy the same knowledge content through clear paraphrase. 4. Use the exact key names from the output schema. Each rubric may return only rubric_id and rubric_text.

sections.title: User Prompt
sections.content: For each relationship record in the following list, generate one rubric object based on the provided Wikipedia page evidence. edge_rubric_inputs: {edge_rubric_inputs} Return ONLY JSON. J.2 Evaluation Prompt J.2.1 Judge Prompt System Prompt You need to evaluate whether report covers set of predefined scoring points. The input will include user research question, several rubric objects, and the report to be evaluated. Each rubric object represents one specific knowledge point to check, and rubric_text is the only scoring criterion. Your task is to judge, item by item, whether the report satisfies the corresponding rubric_text, and to provide brief reason for each judgment. Return only JSON that conforms to the required schema. Rules: 1. Score each rubric object using only its rubric_text and three-tier scoring scheme: 1 means satisfied, 0.5 means partially satisfied, and 0 means not satisfied. Base your judgment only on what is explicitly present in the report. Do not use external knowledge, common-sense completion, or subjective inference. 2. Assign 1 when the report explicitly states or clearly paraphrases the knowledge required by the rubric, covering the key facts, relationships, qualifiers, or numerical details required by the rubric. Reasonable paraphrases are acceptable, but the rubric must be substantively satisfied. 3. Assign 0.5 when the report mentions the core object, relationship, or fact required by the rubric and covers at least one substantive key element, but misses other key elements, qualifiers, dates, numerical values, causal links, or necessary context. General discussion of related topic, mere mention of related terms, or content that does not cover any specific knowledge required by the rubric is not enough for 0.5. 4. Assign 0 when the report does not mention the specific knowledge required by the rubric, only discusses related topic generally, or makes factual statement that contradicts the rubric. If the reports core factual claim contradicts the rubric, assign 0 rather than 0.5, even if related content is mentioned. 5. For every input rubric object, return exactly one object in rubric_results, and preserve the original rubric_id exactly. Do not omit, merge, rewrite, or add rubrics. 6. Each result must contain only rubric_id, score, and reason. The reason should briefly explain why the rubric is satisfied, partially satisfied, or not satisfied, and should indicate which key elements the report covered, which key elements it missed, or which fact contradicts the rubric. 7. Keep each reason within 50 words. User Prompt Please formally score report against provided rubric set. query: {query} The report to evaluate is provided in the next message. The rubric_objects to score are provided after the report. When asked to respond, return only JSON. Each rubric result must contain only rubric_id, score, and reason. 47 # Report To Evaluate {report_text} rubric_objects: {rubric_objects_json} Now evaluate the report against exactly the rubric object(s) listed above. Use only the provided rubric ids. score must be one of: - 1: The report explicitly states or clearly paraphrases the knowledge required by the rubric and covers the key elements - 0.5: The report covers some substantive key elements of the rubric, but misses other necessary elements or qualifiers - 0: The report does not mention the specific knowledge, is only generally related, or factually contradicts the rubric Each reason must be concise: within 50 words. Return ONLY JSON.
